definition: A model of a test suite with four layers: static analysis, unit, integration and end-to-end tests. It is widest at integration, which usually gives the most confidence for its cost.
A test that checks one function or module in isolation, usually in milliseconds. Ideal for pure logic with many edge cases, such as rounding money.
A test that checks several units working together, such as a form component using the real parsing code with a faked network. It catches wiring bugs unit tests miss.
A test that drives the real application in a real browser, through the UI, API and data layer. The most realistic and the most expensive kind of test.
Vitest's default locally: after a run it waits, and when you save a file it reruns only the tests affected by that change, using Vite's module graph.
A three-part shape for tests: build the inputs, perform the one action under test, then state what should now be true. It makes tests easy to scan.
A check inside a test that throws when a value is not what you expected, such as `expect(total).toBe(1000)`. A test fails when an assertion throws.
How code produces its result (private helpers, internal state, call order), as opposed to the behaviour callers observe. Tests coupled to it break on harmless refactors.
A property that holds for every valid input, such as "the shares add up to the total". Asserting an invariant across several inputs catches whole families of bugs.
Testing inputs just below, on and just above each limit in a rule, such as 0 and 0.01 or two and three decimals, because bugs cluster at those edges.
A test written once and run for each row of a table of inputs and expected outputs. In Vitest, `test.each` creates one named test per row.
A stand-in collaborator that returns canned answers so a test can control a dependency, for example an API object whose `post` method always resolves with an id.
Any stand-in for a real collaborator in a test: stubs return canned answers, spies record calls, mocks are spies you assert on, and fakes are simpler working versions.
A function or method wrapper that records how it was called. `vi.spyOn(object, method)` watches a real method and can also override it until restored.
A test clock that replaces `setTimeout`, `setInterval` and `Date`, so tests can skip ahead with calls like `vi.advanceTimersByTime(2000)` instead of waiting in real time.
The name assistive technology announces for an element, computed from `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, an associated label or its text. Role queries match on it.
Testing Library's recommended order for finding elements: by role, label, placeholder, text or display value first; then alt text and title; test ids last.
A Testing Library package that simulates whole user interactions, including pointer, focus and keyboard events, instead of dispatching single events like `fireEvent` does.
An asynchronous Testing Library query that retries until a matching element appears, resolving with it or rejecting after a timeout (one second by default).
A library that intercepts network requests in Node and the browser and answers them with handlers you define, so your real fetch and data code still run in tests.
In Playwright, a lazy, strict description of how to find an element, such as `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`. It is resolved again on every action.
A Playwright assertion on a locator, such as `toHaveText`, that re-checks the page until it passes or times out, instead of reading a value once.
In Playwright, a value a test requests by name, like `page` or a custom `group`, with setup before `use()` and teardown after it, created only for tests that need it.
A Playwright recording of a test run with every action, DOM snapshots before and after it, console output and network calls, opened in the trace viewer.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change, usually because of timing, shared data or uncontrolled time. It teaches teams to ignore failures.
Writing one failing test, making it pass with the simplest code, then refactoring with the tests green, in short repeated cycles known as red, green, refactor.
The share of statements, branches, functions and lines that ran during the tests. It shows untested code but not whether the executed code was actually checked.
Grading a test suite by making small deliberate bugs (mutants) in the code and rerunning the tests; killed mutants were caught, survived mutants reveal weak tests.
A mutant whose change does not alter any behaviour a caller could observe, so no reasonable test can kill it. It should be ignored, not chased.
A CI job that must pass before a pull request can merge into a protected branch, turning the test pipeline from a suggestion into a gate.
